T2: Thermal oscillations
A resistor undergoes a phase transition. Its resistance is \(R_1\) below temperature \(T_c\), and \(R_2>R_1\) above \(T_c\). It is connected to a voltage source through an inductor of inductance \(L\). If the applied voltage lies between two critical values, \(V_1<V<V_2\), the resistor temperature oscillates.

Assume (i) the heat flux to the ambient medium is \(P=\alpha(T-T_0)\), where \(\alpha\) is constant and \(T_0\) is ambient temperature, and (ii) the resistor is small enough to reach thermal equilibrium much faster than \(L/R_2\).
a
Express \(V_1\) and \(V_2\) in terms of the supplied parameters.
b
For \(V_1<V<V_2\), sketch qualitatively \(T(t)\), and find \((T_{\max}-T_0)/(T_{\min}-T_0)\).
c
Find the oscillation period when \(V=\sqrt{V_1V_2}\) and \(R_2=16R_1\).

Instantaneous thermal balance gives \(T=T_0+R I^2/\alpha\). Define switching currents \(I_1=\sqrt{\alpha(T_c-T_0)/R_1}\) and \(I_2=\sqrt{\alpha(T_c-T_0)/R_2}\), and branch equilibrium currents \(J_j=V/R_j\). On the low-resistance branch the current rises towards \(J_1>I_1\) with time constant \(L/R_1\). At \(I_1\), temperature reaches \(T_c\) and resistance switches to \(R_2\). solution.text:
T2: Thermal oscillations
a. Critical voltages
At constant resistance \(R_j\), equilibrium requires \(V^2/R_j=\alpha(T_{\rm eq}-T_0)\). A nonoscillating state must have \(T_{\rm eq}<T_c\) on branch 1 or \(T_{\rm eq}>T_c\) on branch 2. Thus
\[V_1=\sqrt{R_1\alpha(T_c-T_0)},\qquad V_2=\sqrt{R_2\alpha(T_c-T_0)}.\]
b. Temperature and current
Instantaneous thermal balance gives \(T=T_0+R I^2/\alpha\). Define switching currents \(I_1=\sqrt{\alpha(T_c-T_0)/R_1}\) and \(I_2=\sqrt{\alpha(T_c-T_0)/R_2}\), and branch equilibrium currents \(J_j=V/R_j\). On the low-resistance branch the current rises towards \(J_1>I_1\) with time constant \(L/R_1\). At \(I_1\), temperature reaches \(T_c\) and resistance switches to \(R_2\). Current is continuous across the switch, so temperature jumps upwards. It then decreases as current tends towards \(J_2<I_2\), with time constant \(L/R_2\). At \(I_2\), temperature reaches \(T_c\) from above and jumps down as resistance switches back to \(R_1\).


The ideal jumps represent the negligible thermal-response-time limit. Between switches \(I\) is an exponential relaxation, while \(T-T_0=R I^2/\alpha\) is proportional to its square. The extrema occur immediately after switching:
\[T_{\max}-T_0=\frac{R_2 I_1^2}{\alpha},\quad T_{\min}-T_0=\frac{R_1 I_2^2}{\alpha},\quad \frac{T_{\max}-T_0}{T_{\min}-T_0}=\left(\frac{R_2}{R_1}\right)^2.\]
c. Period
On branch \(j\), with initial current \(I_{\rm start}\), \(I(t)=J_j+(I_{\rm start}-J_j)e^{-R_jt/L}\). The two branch durations give
\[\mathcal T=\frac L{R_1}\ln\frac{I_2-J_1}{I_1-J_1}+\frac L{R_2}\ln\frac{I_1-J_2}{I_2-J_2}.\]
With \(\eta=R_2/R_1=16\), \(V=\eta^{1/4}\sqrt{R_1\alpha(T_c-T_0)}\). Hence \(I_2=I_1/4\), \(J_1=2I_1\), \(J_2=I_1/8\), and
\[\mathcal T=\frac L{R_1}\left[\ln\left(\frac74\right)+\frac1{16}\ln7\right]\simeq0.6812\frac L{R_1}.\]
